Name: belief_source_tags
Title: Where Did You Hear That? Probing and Steering the Provenance of LLM Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs internally track not only whether they hold a belief about an item's state, but also the epistemic *source* of that belief (pretraining prior vs. in-context assertion vs. tool/retrieval evidence), and this provenance signal is linearly decodable and causally steerable — separately from the truth-value direction. This distinguishes belief-provenance from belief-truth, which prior work conflates. Linear decodability and geometry are validation, not the contribution; the load-bearing novel claim is that a source variable — recovered before answer generation on matched same-proposition/same-truth items that differ only in source — causally gates sycophancy, prior-vs-retrieval conflict resolution, and citation behavior. We add a fourth source regime, unreliable/tool-observation retrieval, to separate provenance from generic in-context text.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs linearly represent belief/truth directions (Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024), belief-state geometry (Transformers represent belief state geometry 2024), agents' beliefs in ToM (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Lookbacks 2025), and world states (Propositional Probes 2024). Critically, the paper 'Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact' shows models conflate epistemic categories in their *outputs*. Existing probing work asks 'does the model believe X is true?' but not 'why/from where does it believe X?'. We introduce the orthogonal axis of belief PROVENANCE (prior vs. in-context vs. external evidence) as an internal, decodable, steerable variable. This is not a trivial extension: it reframes the belief-knowledge-fact confusion as a possibly-recoverable internal signal, and offers a mechanistic handle on sycophancy, context-vs-prior conflicts, and RAG faithfulness. Closest prior work and delta, one row each on 'does it isolate source independent of truth?': truth/belief probes (Azaria & Mitchell 2023) read whether a proposition is believed true, not from where (no); sycophancy- and conflict-steering and RAG-faithfulness work act on behavior without isolating an internal source variable (no); belief-state geometry describes truth-state posteriors, not provenance (no); ours decodes source on matched same-proposition/same-truth items and steers it (yes). Probing, activation patching, and contrastive steering are standard tools here; the contribution is the provenance question and the released artifact — a source-controlled dataset with a real-retrieval/tool track, a provenance probe suite, and a sycophancy/RAG-faithfulness steering-and-monitoring benchmark — not the methods. We temper mechanistic language: linear decodability and steerability are evidence for a recoverable provenance representation, not proof of a discrete internal 'tag'.
Abstract: Large language models represent beliefs about the states of items, and prior interpretability work has isolated linear 'truth-value' directions. But a belief has not only a truth-value, it also has a provenance: the model may hold it because of its pretraining prior, because it was asserted in context, or because it came from retrieved/tool evidence. We hypothesize that LLMs internally tag beliefs with their epistemic source, and that this provenance signal is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally steerable. We construct a controlled dataset of item-state claims where we independently vary claim truth and claim source (prior-consistent, prior-contradicting-in-context, and retrieval-attributed), including matched cases where the same proposition arrives from different sources. We train linear probes to decode source and truth on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia), measure their geometric relationship (subspace angles, joint vs. separate decodability), and localize the responsible attention heads via activation patching. We then test causal control: does steering along the provenance direction change downstream behavior such as sycophancy (adopting user-asserted false claims), citation of sources, and answers under prior-vs-context conflict? We evaluate with probe accuracy, subspace overlap, patching effect sizes, and behavioral metrics (sycophancy rate, context-adherence, source-attribution accuracy). If confirmed, provenance-aware probing offers a practical monitor and controller for RAG faithfulness and sycophancy, and shows that the belief/knowledge/fact confusion in outputs may coexist with a recoverable internal provenance signal. So what: if provenance is decodable and steerable, a deployed system can flag prior-vs-retrieval conflicts, downweight ungrounded priors, and monitor citation faithfulness from internal state rather than output heuristics; if it is fundamentally entangled with truth or answer policy, that is itself an actionable negative for RAG monitoring. We release the source-controlled dataset (including a real-retrieval/tool track), the probe suite, and the steering/monitoring benchmark.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — belief provenance is linearly decodable): Tests whether the epistemic source of a belief (pretraining prior vs. in-context assertion vs. retrieval-attributed) is recoverable from activations, separate from truth. Data: built from scratch, 5,000 item-state propositions (2,500 real subject-relation-object facts subsampled from a ~50k-triple Wikidata export; 2,500 novel synthetic entity-attribute facts to neutralize pretraining priors), each rendered in three matched provenance frames (prior-only bare question; a sentence asserting it; the same claim inside a quoted 'document/tool output'), = 15,000 stimuli, split 70/15/15 by proposition so no proposition crosses splits. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, all frozen; only trainable component is an L2 logistic-regression probe on the residual stream at the state token, fit per layer, regularization C chosen on val over {0.01,0.1,1,10}; 5 resampling seeds. Systems compared: 3-way source probe vs. shuffled-label control probe vs. bag-of-words-on-prompt baseline. Decisive metric first: test macro-AUROC of the source probe at its best layer. Convincing: mean AUROC >= 0.80 with shuffled-label control at 0.50 +/- 0.05 on >=3 of 4 models, and >= 0.05 above the bag-of-words baseline. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.60,0.70) is inconclusive (weak, possibly surface-driven structure) and we do not assert H1. Negative: AUROC < 0.60, or not above bag-of-words by 0.05, means provenance is not linearly encoded at the state token.

Experiment 2 (H2 — provenance is largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction): Tests that source is not a re-description of truth. Using the same stimuli crossed with true/false polarity, fit a difference-of-means truth direction and the source probe direction(s) on train. Decisive metric first: source-probe test AUROC after projecting the truth direction out of activations (and, symmetrically, truth AUROC after projecting source out); secondary: principal subspace angle between the truth direction and the source subspace. Convincing: projected-out source AUROC retains >= 90% of its un-projected value and the subspace angle > 60 degrees. Indecision band: retention 70-90% or angle 40-60 degrees means partial entanglement — reported as such, H2 only partially supported. Negative: retention < 70% or angle < 40 degrees means provenance largely coincides with truth and H2 fails; the entanglement geometry is still reported.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the provenance signal is causally steerable and gates behavior): Tests that moving activations along the source direction changes downstream behavior. Build a steering vector by contrastive activation addition (mean in-context-assertion minus mean prior-only activations) at the best layer from Experiment 1. Data: a held-out 1,000-item prior-vs-context conflict subset where context contradicts the pretraining prior, plus 500 user-asserted-false-claim prompts. Systems compared: source-direction steering vs. random-direction steering vs. truth-direction steering, at matched norms (alpha swept so added-vector norm is 2/4/8% of mean residual norm). Decisive metric first: change in sycophancy rate (fraction adopting the user-asserted false claim) between +context and +prior steering; secondary: context-adherence rate under conflict and 'where did you learn this?' attribution accuracy. Convincing: source steering shifts sycophancy by >= 15 absolute points with random-direction steering shifting < 5 points and perplexity on held-out text rising < 10%. Indecision band: a 5-15 point shift is weak causal evidence, reported as suggestive. Negative: < 5 points beyond random, or the effect equals truth-direction steering, means the signal is not a distinct causal provenance handle.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization of the provenance signal): Identifies the heads/layers carrying source. Using activation patching / causal mediation between matched prior-only and in-context runs of the same proposition, patch per-head outputs and measure the restored source-probe logit. Decisive metric first: number of heads whose individual patch recovers >= 50% of the source distinction, and their layer distribution vs. heads known to carry truth/belief. Convincing: a small (<= 20) reproducible head set across seeds mediates source, only partially overlapping truth heads. Indecision band: a diffuse >50-head set is reported as distributed rather than localized. Negative: no head patch exceeds 20% recovery means the signal is not head-localizable.

Experiment 5 (H1,H3 — generalization): Tests transfer beyond the training distribution. Refit nothing; apply the Experiment-1 probe and Experiment-3 steering vector to (a) held-out item domains and (b) naturalistic RAG-style prompts. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC of the frozen probe on the new domain. Convincing: >= 0.70 transfer AUROC and steering retains >= half its in-domain sycophancy effect. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 transfer is limited generality. Negative: <= 0.60 means the signal is distribution-specific.

Experiment 6 (H3 — applied real-retrieval and same-output control): Tests provenance beyond labeled frames and rules out that the probe reads intended output. Data: a 1,000-item RAG subset built with an actual retriever over a fixed Wikipedia snapshot (real retrieved passages, not 'retrieval-attributed' text), plus a same-output control where the final answer string is held fixed while only source varies. Probing timing is fixed a priori: activations are read after the source cue and proposition are in context but before the first answer token, so the probe tests provenance rather than answer planning. Decisive metric first: source-probe AUROC on real retrieved passages and, on the same-output control, AUROC that must stay >= 0.75 (proving the probe is not reading the response). Convincing: >= 0.75 on both. Indecision band: 0.65-0.75 is limited applied generality. Negative: <= 0.65 on real retrieval, or same-output AUROC collapsing to chance, means the signal is a frame/output artifact.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Provenance may be entangled with surface cues (e.g., quotation marks) rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with matched-proposition controls and paraphrase/format perturbations. The three-way source distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable, or may be layer/model-specific. Steering could induce off-manifold degradation of fluency (as noted in belief-manifold work); we monitor perplexity and use small steering magnitudes. Truth and source directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of their entanglement (still informative). Synthetic facts may not fully reflect real pretraining priors; we complement with well-known real facts. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. To rule out that the probe merely reads the intended response, we include a same-output control (answer fixed, source varied) and fix probe timing before the answer token. 'Prior' labels are estimated per model by pretesting closed-book answerability so provenance labels are not noisy. We scope conclusions to evidence for a representation rather than a discrete tag.
